title: Kuf

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzadi, and Noah, righteous in his generations. Your line was tzadi for tzaddik. Did the one act get done? Today, the letter that begins holy. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

"Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy." That's how Leviticus nineteen begins, in the King James words. It sounds like the start of something about temples and altars. Read on, and there's an offering or two, but mostly something else. The very same chapter tells you to leave the corners of your field for the poor. To pay a worker before the night is out. Not to curse the deaf or trip the blind. To love your neighbor as yourself. Holiness, in this chapter, shows up at the edge of a field and on payday. Today's letter starts the word.
screen: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.` → `THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.` → `PAY THE WORKER TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kuf. It makes a k sound, deep in the back of the mouth, and it begins kadosh, holy. Take it in four steps. First, the root. The root of kadosh carries the sense of set apart, marked off for something. Holy things in Hebrew are not necessarily shiny. They are distinct, given a different use. Second, a day. Early in Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, and in the King James words, "God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Sanctified is that same root. Before the story has a sanctuary or a priest, it has a holy day. Jews meet that root on Friday night in kiddush, the blessing over wine that sets Shabbat apart. Third, a cry. The prophet Isaiah sees angels calling to one another, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Jews say those words in the Kedushah, a part of the prayer service whose very name means holiness, some rising up on their toes as they say them. Fourth, the hands. Back to Leviticus nineteen. The chapter that opens with be holy fills itself with ordinary acts: fair weights, honest wages, respect for the old. Kiddush, Kaddish, Kedushah, kadosh. The same letter and root run through wine, mourning, prayer and law. Leviticus doesn't keep holiness on a mountain. It sets it apart inside a field, a market, a workday. In this reading, something becomes holy when it's given a purpose beyond itself and treated that way.
screen: `KADOSH: SET APART.` · `A DAY MADE HOLY.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY IN THE KEDUSHAH.` · `HOLINESS AT THE EDGE OF A FIELD.` · then, large: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one holy moment. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day. Look for one moment that felt set apart, even slightly. The first sip of coffee in a quiet kitchen. A child's hand in yours. A fair deal honestly made. A stranger who held a door. It doesn't need to be religious to count. Hold that moment for a few breaths, and ask what made it different from the minutes around it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Kuf. The letter of kadosh, holy, and of kiddush and Kedushah: set apart for a purpose. Today's word.
Your line: kuf for kadosh. Today, set one ordinary moment apart on purpose, and treat it like it matters. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews say the words of Isaiah 6:3 in the Kedushah during the repetition of the Amidah, and make kiddush over wine to set Shabbat apart; Leviticus 19, which opens with "be holy", is read in the yearly Torah cycle.

what it means: set apart for a purpose — a day, a cup of wine, a fair wage.
what a scholar hears: one root, k-d-sh, in Genesis 2:3, Leviticus 19:2, Isaiah 6:3, kiddush, Kaddish and Kedushah.

notes: Leviticus 19:2, Genesis 2:3 and Isaiah 6:3 quoted from KJV. Confirm wording.
'The root of kadosh is usually explained as set apart': standard lexicon gloss, attributed. Confirm.
'Before the story has a sanctuary or a priest, it has a holy day' avoids a 'first' claim but implies one; confirm acceptable.
Rising on the toes during the Kedushah given as 'often'; a widespread custom, not universal. Confirm.
Kaddish included in the k-d-sh family: Kaddish is Aramaic from the same root. Confirm phrasing 'the same letter and root'.
